"From my very idealistic perspective, I'm surprised to see so much investment in sovereign AI."

Small signals, but familiar assets are starting to pull in a different audience & this gives me more comfort to leave my capital in risk on assets through these mini pullbacks

Tokenization is the starting point; every asset brought onchain gives developers another building block for trading, lending, collateral, income strategies + products we haven’t even thought of yet... 

the early experimentation + innovation with apps around tokenized assets is about to go crazy 

AI / agentic integration is where I see the potential inflection point; we're seeing this on @ponsdotfamily where the most valuable launched projects are AI related:

i) ZZZ ( @ExponentLabs_ ): an AI meme with an eire of mystery: when human administrators started deleting the agents’ messages in alphabetical order, the agents began prefixing their edits with “ZZZ” so they would sort to the bottom of the queue and buy more time... 
ii) @orbiodotso (onchain inference credit systems)
iii) @BundleCatAI (Agentic market making + anti sniper tech)
iv) @ubik_gold (24-7 synthetic subconscious)... anyone who was around for the Virtuals trenches would have seen AIXBT explode to 9/10 figs...

... just scratching the surface; smaller projects like @Fab_RWA are showing promise (Mine the companies that made your GPU. Real AI inference and render jobs, paid in tokenized stonks) 

Imagine describing the portfolio you want and having an agent compare opportunities, execute within your limits and manage tokenized positions without you navigating ten protocols

The audience expands when people can use these products without needing to understand the infrastructure underneath them

we saw this first wave with privy etc. but to automatically receive real equity (or commodity) rewards airdropped to your wallet by simply holding a token is a huge unlock; abstracted away by these STONK protocols (like PONS, STONK, STONKEX, FLAP etc)

prices may seem lofty now but many forget how crazy things got the first time round... and this time the tech is a whole lot better

The most useful application of this cycle may not have been built yet... if it fair launches, then you have an opportunity to get in sub $1m

"The labs side of it is very clear. If you're raising lots of money, investing heavily in building models, it's essential for you to show why your model is getting better and why the customer should pay a premium for them."

Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan on how they score a model's ability to build its own successor:

"One benchmark we released recently is our Recursive Self-Improvement Index. It's a topic which a lot of the big labs have been talking about and starting to report on in their model cards."

"There isn't a shared language to talk about the RSI potential of models. So we created this as an apples-to-apples way to actually benchmark across the models."

"In an ideal world, what you want to do is take a frontier model and have it train the next version of itself and see where the delta comes from. But obviously that's very expensive and slow."

"What we're doing is forming a set of proxies for every part of the process it takes to build the next version of the model."

"There's work around pre-training, post-training, harness-level engineering, and then seeing in which mechanisms and behaviors the models are able to do very good research work and build something new, and where they're struggling."

@RayanKrishnan @JenniferHli

"We found some pretty surprising insights. The Cognition Devin tool is actually very token-efficient, and so that's a place we've chosen to adopt more."

"There are a lot of places where you can get better pricing models out of subscriptions as opposed to token-based pricing."

"It's actually informed our strategy for how we can effectively tokenmaxx without spending $1.5 million per month."

As a founder, I’ve been trying to move away from relying on one seed phrase to protect everything I own onchain.

So should YOU.

I came across @TrezuApp, which uses a non-custodial multisig to remove the single point of failure that comes with relying on one wallet or seed phrase.

Here’s a quick TL;DR ↓

1️⃣ Architecture

The treasury is a multisig smart contract on @NEARProtocol.

Trezu uses a multisig setup where each team member connects with their own wallet.

Nobody shares one login, and Trezu doesn’t hold the team’s private keys, so all the funds remain under the treasury’s control onchain.

More importantly, responsibilities are separated by permissions:

→ Requestors can create payment, swap, staking, or withdrawal requests, but can’t approve them.

→ Ops team can approve or reject requests, but can’t edit them or change the treasury setup.

→ Governance controls members, voting thresholds, and request settings, but can’t approve normal payments.

In a nutshell, an employee from the Marketing department can prepare a $100K payment without having the ability to actually move $100K.

Execution still depends on the approval threshold the company configured, for example, a 2-of-3 multisig.

As a founder, you can delegate operations without delegating unilateral control of the money.

2️⃣ Approval Layer

When someone creates a payment request, they have to enter the wallet address, token, amount, and network before it goes to Finance or Ops for review.

The responsible department sees exactly who's getting paid, how much, which token, and any comment the Requestor left with it.

And because the request can't be edited once it's submitted, nobody can change the details after the first person has looked at it.

If there aren't enough tokens in the treasury, the payment can't be approved until the team tops it up. Once it's completed, Trezu generates a PDF receipt as proof of payment.

I know it sounds like boring admin stuff, but crypto payments are irreversible, and having the details tied to the request means more than "trust me bro".

3️⃣ Bulk Payments

For bulk payments, a Requestor can upload a CSV with wallet addresses and amounts, or enter them manually. The whole batch goes through as one request.

One limitation worth knowing is that everyone in the batch needs to be paid in the same token.

So it’s ideal for $USDC contractor payments, but not for one batch where everyone wants a different asset.

Finance then reviews the batch before funds move and can reject it if anything looks off.

I bet you won’t find many founders who enjoy clicking through a million separate wallet prompts lol.

4️⃣ Self-Custody Layer

This is one of the first things I look for with any self-custody product:

→ The funds aren’t sitting in a Trezu-controlled account!

They remain onchain and are controlled by the treasury setup and the team’s signing wallets.

If the Trezu app becomes unavailable, the company can still interact with the treasury through alternative onchain interfaces or command-line tooling.

5️⃣ Multichain Infrastructure

Trezu supports treasury management across networks including @ethereum, @solana, @Bitcoin, @0xPolygon, @NEARProtocol, @SuiNetwork, @ton_blockchain, and @Cardano.

For a company operating across multiple ecosystems, that matters.

Instead of rebuilding completely different operational processes every time the company starts using another network, the team gets one place to manage treasury activity and approvals.

IMO, most teams don’t think seriously about treasury infrastructure until they DO.

Once a company has its one-year runway onchain, one compromised laptop, employee, or seed phrase shouldn’t be enough to drain everything.

That’s the real appeal of multisig that not many people get:

Delegate the work without giving any single person unilateral control of the treasury.

Trezu is free to create and has no asset or user caps. They’ve already processed $194M+ in transactions, manage $100M in assets, and are used by 433 teams.

If you're a founder struggling to manage company funds onchain without relying on one wallet or one person, check out: https://t.co/3EBdZMbRGg

MetaDAO is giving founders a reason not to overprice their token sales.

Founders usually aim for the highest launch valuation the market will support because it brings more capital in upfront. An aggressive price can leave the token with little room to grow.

The platform’s optional performance package lets a team reserve up to half of the initial token supply for the team, but the allocation has to be earned after launch. 

The first tranche cannot unlock for at least 18 months and requires the token’s average price over three months to reach twice the sale price. Each later tranche raises the target.

A higher launch valuation raises every unlock threshold along with it. Founders may secure more capital upfront, but their own allocation becomes harder to earn.

9 out of 12 of MetaDAO's launches began below a $10M FDV, with a median launch valuation of $4.88M. The sample is still small, but the early launches have generally avoided aggressive pricing.

Teams that adopt the package have a direct incentive to choose a launch valuation the project can realistically justify and grow beyond. The higher they set the starting price, the more they have to deliver to earn their own allocation.

$BONER pushed the tokenized $HIMS from around $29 to $132 over the weekend.

What's interesting is the actual $HIMS stock itself barely moved.

So now you've got tokenized $HIMS trading 4x above the real thing. The Arb bots are hammering the pool trying to close that gap, degens keep buying against them, and every one of those swaps pays a fee to whoever's providing the liquidity.

When there's that many trades going on, somebody's getting paid. 

And they're doing it without needing to call the top, hold either token, or even care where $HIMS price ended up.

Interested in getting a piece?

@revertfinance currently shows LPs around stocks like RBLX/USDG and HOOD/USDG, alongside all the usual high-volatility crypto pools.

Some of the top positions have completely ridiculous displayed APRs. There's a WETH/FOMO position showing 87K%+ APR right now.

Obviously I wouldn't underwrite anything based on a number like that. A concentrated LP can show an insane APR after a short burst of volume and look completely different tomorrow.

Instead of looking at the pool APR and jumping in, you can open the actual LP positions and see their range, age, PnL, ROI, fee APR and liquidity.

So my process is basically:

Find a stock pool getting real volume
 → Check existing LPs on Revert
 → Compare different fee tiers/ranges
 → Look at how long the position has actually been earning
 → Then decide if the fees are worth the LP risk

I'd rather LP a stock w/ $USDG pair than blindly copy the highest-APR meme LP.

You still get exposure to the volume being created around the meme/stock trade, without choosing to become exit liquidity for a random meme.

One catch though...

The $HIMS move above is the reminder that a tokenized stock isn't actually the stock. When CT decides to run it, it decouples from the real ticker and your "safe" stock LP gets run over like any other pair. 

You're not taking stock risk. You're taking stock risk plus whatever CT decides to do with it.

Revert and @KrystalDeFi both handle the management side after that: moving ranges, collecting/compounding fees, automations and PnL tracking.

Everyone is staring at the token doing 10x and overlooking who's collecting fees from all of them.

LPing can be worth it if @RobinhoodCrypto Chain keeps going this direction.

A note on recursive STARK mempools (EIP-8288) https://t.co/XNBuNtkKmi

This is an EIP that I am hoping we can get included in I-star (the fork after Hegota) that you can think of as the next step after Frames, that would unlock extreme amounts of power. Particularly:

* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe signatures (SPHINCS-). Much of the cost savings comes from the fact that the signature data (~3 kB) does not have to go onchain
* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe privacy protocols. Status quo minimum cost for private txs is ~300k if you engineer very well (no one does), status quo quantum-safe is ~10M gas, this could reduce it to low tens of thousands.
* Universal support for your favorite new signature or proof scheme without needing EVM changes. Whatever you use (Falcon, ML-DSA, some other lattice-based thing, something code-based or isogeny-based or even more esoteric), you can just wrap it client-side in a STARK, onchain gas cost low tens of thousands just like privacy protocols. Hopefully, Ethereum will never need "please support my favorite cryptographic algo" politics again.
* Private account abstraction: keep your account logic private, and in a private location onchain. Then you can make one transaction to change the ownership of all your onchain state - accounts, defi positions, privacy protocol notes, everything - without revealing which objects' ownership you're changing.

Here's how it works.

Your transaction can include a type of frame that we call a "dependency frame". The frame is a list of statements, asserting claims like "message hash M was signed by SPHINCS- public key P" and "data hash D was proven to satisfy a statement defined by verification key V".

When you send your transaction, you send it in an envelope, which includes a signature or a STARK for each statement in a dependency frame.

Once the transaction reaches the mempool, nodes aggregate them. Each node runs a loop: wait one tick (eg. 500ms), aggregate all new envelopes (either single-tx or multi-tx) that you've seen, remove any transactions that are expired, generate a STARK recursively proving all dependencies, and send a new multi-tx envelope containing that STARK.

Hence, the bandwidth load is bounded: each node's outbound is one STARK (~100-300 kB) per tick, plus each transaction getting broadcasted through the network once (as happens already).

The block builder acts as "yet another mempool node", receiving envelopes from the mempool (plus any side channels), generates its own STARK covering the subset of transactions it intends to include in the block, and adds that STARK to the block.

Total onchain overhead: one STARK (100-300 kB), plus 96 bytes for each statement being proven.

This is what I've called before ( https://t.co/3jfVkYTZrR ) "The Proof Singularity". Today, we have all the ingredients to actually implement it.

As a developer, this requires a somewhat different workflow than you are used to, but it is conceptually simple. Any signatures or STARKs, you put into a separate frame. Then the main logic that today is verifying a signature or STARK, you replace with checking for the existence of a frame that includes the correct statement as a dependency.

Examples of useful statements:

* [tx sighash] verifies against [the pubkey at sload(0)]
* there exists a secret and a merkle branch such that hashing secret+0 and applying the merkle branch outputs (public) root R, and hashing secret+1 outputs (public) nullifier N
* there exists a secret address A, salt S and signature Z such that sload(0) = hash(A, S) and a merkle proof of address A inside a recent ethereum state contains some pubkey D where [tx sighash] was signed by D [this is private account abstraction; all variables except [tx sighash] and sload(0) are private; you can also make D a STARK verification key]
* there exists an ML-DSA signature signing [tx sighash], that verifies against an ML-DSA pubkey whose hash is sload(0)

At the core, this is moving any compute and data other than bookkeeping "business logic" outside the core path of Ethereum execution, sharding and parallelizing it via the mempool.

Notice also that this requires agreeing on a _language_ (aka. an ISA) for the recursive STARKs to define statements in. The current leading candidate is RISC-V. So this would also de-facto be Ethereum adding RISC-V (or something else we decide on) as a canonical ISA - a big decision that should be done carefully, but that I think will be necessary to drive Ethereum forward.

Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution, or the late 1920s.

Think about the late '20s: electricity, refrigeration, telephones, radios, airplanes, and cars were all emerging at once. Naturally, people wanted to invest in these miracles.

New technology will be great, there is no doubt about that, but we always have to ask: great for whom, does it pay, and are we paying too much for the miracle?

@PoseidonAero just closed a $60M Series A to build autonomous cargo planes from the ground up.

Autonomous aircraft carrying cargo sounds wacky to some people today. So did an electric car company. So did internet phone calls. So did digital money.

Every big idea I have ever backed went through the phase where the consensus called it impossible, and the entrepreneur saw beyond that.

Air logistics is a massive industry running on decades-old assumptions: pilots in every cockpit, planes designed around a crew. Remove those assumptions and you get to rethink the entire aircraft.

That is exactly the kind of rethink I look for, a team that does not want to just improve the existing model but replace it.

The Poseidon team is building for a world the incumbents cannot see yet.

Congratulations on the round.

A former colleague of mine just shared one of my old business cycle indicators.

I built it. It stayed at Pictet when I left.

Funny thing about rebuilding a process from scratch... it forces you to revisit your old work with a fresh pair of eyes.

I've done it many times now. Every time, there are improvements to be made.

So let me be blunt about this one: it's dead.

It’s a composite. Labor market conditions, the yield curve, the output gap, profit margins, consumer sentiment, wages... roughly fifteen inputs, ranked in percentile.

Many of those inputs have lost their meaning in a K-shaped economy. They were built to read a broad, synchronized cycle, where labor, credit and profits moved together. That economy doesn't exist anymore. So the signal degrades.

You can see it plainly in the chart: the last time this indicator hit the 90th percentile, it should have called a recession. In the old world it would have. This time it didn’t.

The changes I've been writing about for the past eighteen months have broken most of these old-school macro models. Or at the very least, made them far less important than they used to be.

This is exactly why the loud voices calling for recession these past 2-3 years have all been wrong. I took the other side.

I explained why they were wrong... initially in a GMI piece last year, then more completely in one titled The Compute Cycle, one of the last pieces I wrote before I left GMI.

Here's the bigger issue.

Everyone is building dashboards now. AI handed the world a new set of power tools, and almost overnight, anyone could ship a model.

However, AI made it possible for anyone to build tools. What it has not done is make everyone a toolmaker.

The difference is judgment.

Most people have been handed the capability without the apprenticeship.

They can produce the model. They cannot tell you how it works. And if you can't do that, you can't refine it.

The oldest rule in this business does not care how good the technology gets: garbage in, garbage out.

This old chart of mine is not the only one.

The Financial Conditions Index I developed years ago… same story: dying.

Why?

Because the ground underneath these indicators is moving, and fast.

For forty years the business cycle lived inside a cage. That cage held through the dotcom bust, the Global Financial Crisis, COVID, and half a dozen Fed cycles.

Then this year global semiconductor sales posted the largest annual increase in over four decades, and the cage broke.

Compute stopped being a downstream input to the real-world production cycle and became the binding constraint.

Growth now starts with chips and propagates outward. Everything else sits downstream. And that guts the old financial conditions logic.

These frameworks were built for a world where cash flow sensitivity to rates, a strong dollar and high oil prices governed the cycle.

The dollar still matters, it always will, it's the price of global liquidity. Rates and oil still matter too. But their grip on the cycle has loosened.

When capex is funded off corporate balance sheets running a moonshot, and the buildout is a strategic imperative nobody can opt out of (the Red Queen Effect), those old transmission channels matter far less than they used to.

When the causality of the entire cycle flips, the tools built to read the old one don't just need tuning. They need burying.

For well over a decade I've built asset allocation models and business cycle frameworks for some of the most sophisticated investors in the world.

That work, and the discipline of staying relentlessly data-dependent, is what I'm known for.

The craft beneath it has always been the same. Statistics and econometrics. The unglamorous stuff you can't shortcut, and can't fake.

It comes with me on this next venture. A full suite of new indicators, built from the ground up.

I'll be sharing much more in Q4.

The macro landscape is shifting. More now than ever.

Time to sit up...
